::: {.callout-warning title="Scope and caveats"}
The Down syndrome estimates in this chapter describe a **pooled research sample, not a population**: children with Down syndrome from studies in six countries, recruited through research projects (including an intervention trial), charities and family organisations, and assessed between the 1990s and the 2020s. Families who enrol in such studies are not a random draw of all families of children with Down syndrome, so the reported trajectories and percentiles are expectations for the modelled pool and are **not norms**, cut-offs or a screening instrument.

All outcomes are **parent-report checklist counts**, harmonised from several instruments onto a common 810-item reference inventory (@sec-data). Comprehension is the least direct of the three measures, and everything derived from it — the production ratio $q(a)$, the signing ratio $r(a)$ and total expressive vocabulary — inherits that. A checklist word count says nothing about intelligibility, grammar or use in context, and nothing about which words: a count treats a verb or a function word the same as a noun, and those are the words that grammar is built from (@sec-ds-vocabulary-grammar).

Coverage is **uneven across age**: dense between about 18 and 54 months and thin above 72 months for spoken words and above about 60 for words understood, where the study mix also changes. Estimates at older ages are smoothed by the model from few children and carry correspondingly wide intervals; monthly rows with `n_obs = 0` are extrapolation, not evidence.

The study is **descriptive and exploratory**, not preregistered or confirmatory. Estimates are conditional on the model (@sec-trends, @sec-betabinomial, @sec-randomeffects), health, cognitive level, socio-economic status and intervention exposure are not modelled, and no causal reading is licensed. **Sex is modelled**, as a covariate, from the model definitions of 2026-09-13 onwards (issue [#324](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/324)): girls and boys each sit half a coefficient either side of a sex-balanced midpoint, a child whose sex is not recorded sits at the midpoint, and no administration is dropped. Seven of the fifteen Down syndrome studies, `us_03` among them, record no sex, so the coefficients are estimated from the eight that do and assume the difference is the same in the others; the earlier exploratory variant fitted to those eight studies found girls ahead on both words understood and the production ratio, the larger difference on production ([`notes/202609041530`](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/blob/main/notes/202609041530-vg20-sex-shift-arm.md)). A fit made under the new definitions draws its population trajectories at the sex-balanced midpoint and reports girls' and boys' predictions beside them; a figure from a fit made before then averages over the pool's recorded mix of girls, boys and children of unrecorded sex. When setting expectations for an individual child, quote the **posterior predictive** count ($Y$, $P(Y \le k)$), which carries between-child variability and stays wide, not the expected trajectory ($E[Y]$), which carries parameter uncertainty only (@sec-interval-convention).

Numbers are drawn from the model of record (VG20, which replaced VG10 on 2026-08-19; it differs from VG10 by the child-effect correlation and, from 2026-09-13, the sex covariate) at the canonical 6-monthly ages; see the Discussion (@sec-limitations) for the full statement of limitations.
:::
